items.title: French Natural Horn
items.description: The 18th-century natural horn had no valves and produced notes from the natural harmonic series. Unlike the modern French horn, which has a fully chromatic range of about three and a half octaves, the 18th-century horn could produce only around sixteen natural notes. Its sound was also generally brighter and more open than that of the modern instrument.

items.title: Bartmann Bottle
items.description:
This Bartmann bottle was made in Frechen, Germany, around 1550–1700. Made from durable brown-glazed stoneware, it has a rounded body, narrow neck and sturdy handle for storing and carrying liquids. Its moulded flower medallion reflects the decorative style of Frechen stoneware, which was widely traded across Europe and commonly used in domestic and drinking settings.

The name Bartmann, meaning “bearded man” in German, refers to the distinctive bearded face moulded onto the neck of these vessels. In Britain, Bartmann vessels also became known as “Bellarmine” jugs, a name associated with the Catholic Cardinal Robert Bellarmine. Beyond their everyday use, some Bartmann bottles were later reused as “witch bottles”, filled with materials such as pins, nails or hair and concealed or buried as protective objects against witchcraft. Over time, this widely traded domestic object acquired additional religious, symbolic and ritual meanings within British social life.

Source: Wikipedia, “Bartmann jug”.

items.title: Cockerel
items.description: A small moulded cockerel-shaped object from the Whitechapel material displayed by UCL. Its surviving form shows a standing bird with textured feathers and a broken pedestal or base. It offers evidence of the small decorative and personal objects found alongside tavern, household and leisure material at the site.

items.title: Domino
items.description: This small ivory domino dates from the late 18th to early 19th century. Its value is marked by recessed circular pips on either side of the central dividing line. Dominoes were popular pieces for social tabletop games, introduced to Europe in the mid-18th century and reaching England by the end of the century. Their hard ivory surfaces produced a distinctive click when placed or moved across a wooden table.

items.title: Mallet Bottle
items.description: This half-size mallet-type glass wine bottle comes from the Whitechapel assemblage. Its squat cylindrical body, long narrow neck and applied rim match a form used to store and serve drink in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. The iridescent weathering visible on the glass is typical of archaeological burial conditions.

items.title: Punch Whistle
items.description:
This 19th-century whistle is made from white metal and shaped as Punch, the well-known comic character associated with British Punch and Judy performances. Although small and decorative, it was also designed to produce a clear, piercing whistle. Its combination of sound and playful figurative design reflects the popular entertainment culture of the period.

Punch developed from Pulcinella, a character from the Italian commedia dell’arte tradition, and became established in Britain from the seventeenth century. By the nineteenth century, Punch and Judy had become a familiar form of popular entertainment, with Punch’s humor often centered on disorder and exaggerated violence, including violence towards his wife Judy. Some nineteenth-century versions also included racial stereotypes, such as the character of Jim Crow, drawing on the blackface minstrel traditions of the period. Over time, Punch has been increasingly criticized for representations of domestic violence, racial stereotypes and violence in children’s entertainment.

Sources: Wikipedia, “Punch and Judy”; Victoria and Albert Museum, “That’s the way to do it: A history of Punch and Judy”.
